body.support:
Every message is **written by someone, for a reason**. A text from your coach tells you about training. An ad wants you to buy. A scam wants to **trick you**.

Scammers think about **who** will read the message. They think about **what** they want you to do. Then they pick words to make you act fast.

Most scams use **4 red flags**:

1. **Rush** — “Do it now!”
2. **Reaction** — They make you scared, excited or sad.
3. **Request** — They want money, a code or a click.
4. **Random** — Something is odd. A number you don’t know. A strange link.

Two or more red flags? **Watch out.**

What should you do? **Stop. Check. Protect.** Don’t reply. Check with the real person or company. Use a number you **already** have. Then block it and tell someone.
body.core:
Every message you get was **written by someone, for a reason**. A text from your coach tells you when training is on. An ad tries to make you buy something. A scam tries to **trick you**.

Scammers are good writers. They think hard about **who will read the message** (the audience) and **what they want the reader to do** (the purpose). Then they choose words that push you to act fast.

Most scams use the same four tricks. We call them the **4 red flags**:

1. **Rush** — “Act now!” “Last chance!” They don’t want you to have time to think.
2. **Reaction** — They make you feel scared, excited or sorry for someone. Big feelings switch off careful thinking.
3. **Request** — They want something: money, a gift card, a code, your password, or a click.
4. **Random** — Something doesn’t fit. A number you don’t know. A strange link. Spelling that’s a bit off. They don’t use your name.

One red flag doesn’t always mean scam. Your mate might really be in a rush! But **two or more red flags is a big warning**.

The best move? **Stop. Check. Protect.** Don’t reply to the message. Check by contacting the person or company another way — use a number or app you *already* have, not the one in the message. Then block, report and tell someone.
body.extend:
Every message you get was **written by someone, for a reason**. A text from your coach tells you when training is on. An ad tries to make you buy something. A scam tries to **trick you**.

Scammers are good writers. They think hard about **who will read the message** (the audience) and **what they want the reader to do** (the purpose). Then they choose words that push you to act fast.

Most scams use the same four tricks. We call them the **4 red flags**:

1. **Rush** — “Act now!” “Last chance!” They don’t want you to have time to think.
2. **Reaction** — They make you feel scared, excited or sorry for someone. Big feelings switch off careful thinking.
3. **Request** — They want something: money, a gift card, a code, your password, or a click.
4. **Random** — Something doesn’t fit. A number you don’t know. A strange link. Spelling that’s a bit off. They don’t use your name.

One red flag doesn’t always mean scam. Your mate might really be in a rush! But **two or more red flags is a big warning**.

The best move? **Stop. Check. Protect.** Don’t reply to the message. Check by contacting the person or company another way — use a number or app you *already* have, not the one in the message. Then block, report and tell someone.

**Why it works.** Scammers use the same techniques as advertisers: urgency, emotive language and a clear call to action. Some scams copy the logo, layout and tone of real companies so the message looks *credible*. Reading critically means asking not just *what* a message says, but *how* it is trying to position you — and who benefits if you do what it asks.

body.support:
In 2022, lots of people in Australia got a text: *“Hi Mum, I lost my phone. This is my new number.”* Then the “child” asked for money.

It was a scam. The ACCC is a government group that protects shoppers. It said that in 7 months of 2022, **more than 1,150 people** were tricked. They lost **$2.6 million**.

Most of them were **parents and grandparents over 55**. They loved their kids and wanted to help fast.

The ACCC says: if you get a text from a new number, **call the person on the number you already have**.
body.core:
In 2022, a scam message spread across Australia. It went like this: *“Hi Mum, I’ve lost my phone. This is my new number.”* After a few friendly messages, the “child” asked for money to pay an urgent bill.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said that in the first seven months of 2022, **more than 1,150 Australians fell for it** and lost **$2.6 million**. Most of the reports came in June and July.

Most people who were tricked were **parents and grandparents over 55**. The scammers knew their audience: people who love their kids and want to help them fast.

The ACCC’s advice: if you get a message from a number you don’t know, **check by calling the person on the number you already have** for them.

source.name: ACCC media release — “ACCC warning of suspicious messages as ‘Hi Mum’ scams spike” (2022)

caseStudies.title: “Earn $500 a day liking videos”

body.support:
Some scams look like a job. A message says: *“Earn $500 a day liking videos!”* At first they might pay you a little. Then they ask **you** to pay money to earn more. That money is gone.

These scams trick people who want work — like young people looking for a first job. **A real job never asks you to pay to start.**
body.core:
Scamwatch warns about fake job offers sent by text, WhatsApp and social media. They promise easy money for simple tasks, like liking videos or rating products. At first, they might even pay you a little bit — so it feels real. Then they ask you to **pay money to “unlock” bigger earnings**. That money is gone.

These scams target people who want work — including young people looking for their first job. **Real jobs never ask you to pay to start.**

teacher.overview:
Students learn that every text is written for a **purpose** and an **audience**, then apply this to scam messages. The literacy core is critical reading: identifying purpose, recognising persuasive techniques (urgency, emotive language, requests) and **inferring** unstated intent. They finish by writing a short warning message for a chosen audience, which gives evidence of adjusting language for audience.

The hook is strong because the main targets of ‘Hi Mum’ scams were parents and grandparents — students become the **expert protector**, not the victim.
prep: Print workbooks (A4, colour if possible — greyscale still works).
Load the explainer on the board (Watch tab) — it reads itself aloud.
Optional: screenshot 2–3 real scam texts you have received (remove personal info).
Check scamwatch.gov.au for the latest local scam alerts to use as a warm-up.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Every text wants something
steps: **Hook (5 min):** Show the ‘Hi Mum’ text on the board. Ask: *Would your mum or nan fall for this? Why?*
**Explicit teaching (15 min):** Purpose and audience. Model with 3 everyday texts (coach text, ad, scam). Think aloud: *Who wrote this? Who for? What do they want me to do?*
**Vocab (10 min):** Word Power page. Say each word aloud together; students use it in a sentence about their own phone.
**Exit:** Each student names one purpose and one audience for a text they saw today.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — The 4 red flags
steps: **Explicit teaching (15 min):** Model annotating the scam text — circle, label, explain. Think aloud for each flag.
**Read (15 min):** ‘Scammers are writers’ — read aloud or partner read; students use the app’s read-aloud if needed. Complete ‘Check your reading’.
**We do → you do (20 min):** ‘Find the red flags’ then ‘Scam or legit?’ in pairs. Discuss the myGov card — *it depends* is a valid answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Reading between the lines
steps: **Case study (15 min):** Read the ‘Hi Mum’ case study together. Highlight the facts (numbers, who, when).
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** Inference = clues + what I know. Model the first row of ‘Read between the lines’.
**Independent (25 min):** Inference table, Stop. Check. Protect., and scenarios.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Protect someone
steps: **Model (10 min):** Write a warning text to an imaginary nan on the board. Show how tone changes for a nan vs a mate.
**Write (25 min):** Final mission. Fast finishers do Level Up.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** Quick check on the app, reflection page, request sign-off.

keyPoints: Purpose = what the writer wants. Audience = who it’s written for.
The 4 red flags: Rush, Reaction, Request, Random. Two or more = big warning.
Inference = clues in the text + what you already know.
Always verify through a channel you already trust — never the link/number in the message.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** purpose = to get your money, info or a click. Flags = Rush, Reaction, Request, Random. Big feelings stop careful thinking. The number in the message might belong to the scammer.

**Find the red flags:** Unknown number (Random); “dropped my phone 😩” (Reaction); “pay this bill” (Request); “today… Pls hurry” (Rush).

**Scam or legit?** AusPost — Scam. Coach Dan — Legit. PS5 — Scam. myGov — Not sure/depends (legit only if the student requested a code; never share it). Job offer — Scam. Mum — Legit.

**Case study:** 1,150+ people, $2.6 million (Jan–Jul 2022); audience = parents/grandparents (mostly over 55); it works because it triggers love/worry (reaction) and urgency.

**Read between the lines (sample):** “Only 2 hours left” → don’t take time to think or check. “Account will be locked” → be scared so you click without checking. “No experience needed” → too good to be true; they want something from you.
